name: Service Design, Scoping and Pricing
description: What a service is, catalogue tiers, discovery and qualifying, scoping and statements of work, change control, estimation, pricing models, margin and utilisation, proposals, contract concepts, delivery governance, support and service levels, upsell and renewal, complaint recovery and subcontracting.
roles: sales,account manager,project manager,delivery manager,cto,ceo,full stack developer

cards.subject: Service
says: delivers an outcome through work performed for the client
cannot be stored or handed over as a finished object before it is performed
depends heavily on the time and skill of the people delivering it
cards.use: sell work that a team performs rather than an item the client takes away
not: is a physical item shipped to the client

cards.subject: Product
says: is built once and sold repeatedly in much the same form
scales without adding delivery time for each extra buyer
cards.use: want to sell the same finished offer to many buyers without redoing the work
not: has to be rebuilt from scratch for every buyer

cards.subject: Productised service
says: packages a repeatable service with a fixed scope, price and timeline
lets sales quote quickly because the steps are standardised
cards.use: want a service that can be sold from a page without a long scoping process
not: is custom designed after a long discovery for each client

cards.subject: Bespoke engagement
says: is shaped around one client's particular needs
needs discovery before it can be priced
cards.use: meet a need that no standard package covers
not: is sold at a fixed catalogue price to every buyer

cards.subject: Deliverable
says: is a tangible output the client receives, such as a site or report
is named in the scope so both sides know what will be handed over
cards.use: need to name exactly what the client will receive at the end of a phase
not: is the business change the client hopes to see

cards.subject: Outcome
says: is the change in the client's business that the work is meant to cause
can be influenced by the service but is rarely fully controlled by the provider
cards.use: want to describe the result the client cares about rather than the items delivered
not: is any document produced during delivery

cards.subject: Managed service
says: takes over the ongoing running of something for a recurring fee
stays accountable for results after the initial build
cards.use: offer to operate a client's hosting or automation month after month rather than hand it over
not: ends when the first deliverable is accepted

cards.subject: Service blueprint
says: maps what the client sees and the behind-the-scenes steps that support it
shows the points where the client and the provider interact
exposes handoffs where delivery can fail
cards.use: want to find where a service breaks down between client-facing and back-office work
not: is the price list for a package

cards.subject: Service catalogue
says: lists the services offered with a description and entry terms
gives sales and clients one consistent view of what can be bought
cards.use: need a single place that shows what the company sells and in what packages
not: records the hours each person has worked

cards.subject: Free tier
says: offers a limited version or audit at no charge
exists to build trust and to qualify buyers
cards.use: want prospects to experience value before any commitment
not: covers the full scope at a discounted price

cards.subject: Semi-free tier
says: gives part of the offer free and charges for the remainder
passes the paid portion's real cost on to the buyer
cards.use: want to give a free starting piece but charge for the work that costs real effort
not: charges the same fee as the paid tier but with less support

cards.subject: Paid tier
says: sells a defined package for a stated fee
sets the standard scope that most buyers are expected to choose
cards.use: sell a standard package that most clients can buy without negotiation
not: is built from scratch for each buyer

cards.subject: Custom tier
says: builds scope and price for the individual client after discovery
is for needs the standard packages cannot cover
cards.use: meet a request that falls outside every published package
not: is priced from a fixed public list

cards.subject: Enterprise tier
says: adds security review, procurement steps and negotiated terms for large buyers
usually brings named contacts and formal service levels
cards.use: sell to a large organisation that insists on its own contract terms and vendor checks
not: is the cheapest self-serve package

cards.subject: Good-better-best
says: presents three graded packages side by side
steers many buyers towards the middle option
cards.use: want to let buyers compare graded options on one page
not: offers a single package with no alternatives

cards.subject: Add-on
says: is an optional extra priced separately from the base package
lets a buyer expand a package without changing tier
cards.use: want to offer an optional extra such as more pages or an extra report
not: is included in every package at no cost

cards.subject: Bundle
says: combines several services at one combined price
raises adoption of services the buyer might not have bought alone
cards.use: want to sell hosting, support and SEO together as one offer
not: sells one service with optional extras

cards.subject: Tier fence
says: is a real difference between tiers that stops buyers who need more from choosing the cheaper tier
protects higher tiers from being undercut by lower ones
cards.use: find that buyers with large needs keep choosing the cheapest package
not: is a limit on how many clients can be served at once

cards.subject: Discovery call
says: gathers the client's goals, constraints and context before any quote
is led by questions rather than a presentation
cards.use: meet a new lead for the first time and need to understand the real need
not: is a call to close the sale on the first contact

cards.subject: Qualifying
says: decides whether a lead is worth pursuing
tests fit, need and ability to buy before time is spent on a proposal
cards.use: need to avoid spending days on a proposal for a lead that cannot buy
not: is the final negotiation of price

cards.subject: BANT
says: checks budget, authority, need and timeline
gives a quick checklist for lead fit
cards.use: want a simple four-part checklist to judge whether a lead is ready
not: measures client satisfaction after delivery

cards.subject: Ideal client profile
says: describes the type of client the service serves best and most profitably
helps decide which leads to chase and which to decline
cards.use: want to focus marketing and sales on the clients who are the best fit
not: is a list of all current clients

cards.subject: Stakeholder mapping
says: identifies who signs, who influences and who can block a decision
reveals whether the person on the call can actually approve spend
cards.use: suspect the person you are talking to is not the final decision maker
not: lists the tasks in the delivery plan

cards.subject: Red-flag lead
says: shows warning signs such as refusing to share goals or expecting enterprise results on a tiny budget
predicts scope disputes and late payment
cards.use: notice a prospect who haggles over price before any scope is discussed
not: is a lead that has asked for a discount

cards.subject: Budget conversation
says: raises a realistic budget range early in discovery
lets the provider propose options that fit rather than guess
cards.use: keep proposing work the client cannot afford
not: happens only after the contract is signed

cards.subject: Discovery summary
says: writes down what was learned and sends it back to the client to confirm
prevents misunderstandings from reaching the proposal
cards.use: want written proof that you and the client heard the same needs
not: is the signed statement of work

cards.subject: No-bid decision
says: declines an engagement that fits badly or carries too much risk
protects delivery capacity for better-fit work
cards.use: face a lead that needs skills you lack and a deadline you cannot meet
not: means losing a deal on price

cards.subject: Scope of work
says: lists what will be done and what will not
sets the boundary against which extra requests are judged
cards.use: need to define the edges of what the client is paying for
not: lists the provider's internal costs

cards.subject: Statement of work
says: names the deliverables, timeline, fees and responsibilities for one engagement
is usually issued under a wider master agreement
cards.use: need a signed document that fixes what one engagement includes
not: sets the general terms that cover all future work

cards.subject: Assumption
says: states a condition taken as true that the estimate depends on
gives a reason to revisit price when the condition proves false
cards.use: know the estimate depends on the client supplying content by a certain date
not: names work that is excluded

cards.subject: Exclusion
says: names something explicitly out of scope
removes doubt over work the client might assume was included
cards.use: want to make clear that ongoing content writing is not part of the build
not: states a condition the estimate relies on

cards.subject: Client dependency
says: is an input the client must supply, such as content, access or approvals
can delay the schedule when it is late
cards.use: need access and approvals from the client before work can proceed
not: is a task the provider completes alone

cards.subject: Work breakdown structure
says: splits deliverables into smaller tasks that can be estimated
supports bottom-up estimating
cards.use: must estimate a large project and need to decompose it into tasks first
not: is a list of the client's stakeholders

cards.subject: Scope baseline
says: is the approved scope against which later changes are measured
is updated only through an approved change
cards.use: need an agreed reference point to judge whether a request is a change
not: is the first rough idea shared in discovery

cards.subject: Paid discovery
says: sells a small scoping engagement before the main project
produces a researched scope and estimate the client can keep
cards.use: face a large unclear project that cannot be priced safely from a short call
not: is an unpaid sales meeting

cards.subject: Success metric
says: defines how the client will judge that the work achieved its aim
is agreed before the work starts
cards.use: need the client to say in numbers what a good result looks like
not: is the number of hours worked

cards.subject: Scope creep
says: is the gradual growth of work with no matching change to fee or time
often arrives as many small requests that each seem minor
cards.use: see the project filling with small extras no one priced
not: is a formally approved scope change

cards.subject: Change request
says: is a formal ask to alter agreed scope
starts the process of costing and approving a change
cards.use: hear the client ask for a feature that was not in the agreed scope
not: is a bug report about agreed work

cards.subject: Change order
says: is the signed approval of a priced scope change
adjusts fee, timeline or both once approved
cards.use: want written approval of the extra cost and time before starting extra work
not: is the client's first informal wish list

cards.subject: Impact assessment
says: sizes the effect of a change on cost, time and risk
lets the client decide with full information
cards.use: need to say what a client's late change will cost in time and money
not: is the review held after delivery

cards.subject: Gold plating
says: is the team adding unrequested extras beyond the agreed scope
raises cost and risk without the client having asked
cards.use: see a developer adding features nobody requested
not: is a client request for more features

cards.subject: Change control
says: routes every change through request, assessment and approval
stops work starting on unapproved changes
cards.use: need a defined path so that no extra work is started on a verbal ask
not: is a way to avoid ever accepting changes

cards.subject: Scope trade-off
says: swaps new work for existing work to hold the fee and date
keeps the budget unchanged by dropping something of equal size
cards.use: hear the client want an addition but refuse more budget or time
not: adds the work and absorbs the cost

cards.subject: Defect versus change
says: separates work that fails the agreed specification from work that adds to it
treats the first as a warranty fix and the second as a paid change
cards.use: hear a client call a new request a bug and expect it free
not: treats every client request as a paid change

cards.subject: Silent absorption
says: is taking on extras without recording them
hides the true cost of serving the client from management and sets a precedent
cards.use: find a team doing unrecorded favours for a client month after month
not: is a documented and approved concession

cards.subject: Bottom-up estimate
says: adds up estimates for each small task
takes longer to prepare but is usually more accurate when tasks are known
cards.use: have a clear task list and need an accurate figure
not: compares the job to a similar past project

cards.subject: Top-down estimate
says: starts from a total budget or time and divides it among parts
is quick and suited to early, low-detail stages
cards.use: have a fixed budget from the client and need to see what fits
not: adds detailed task estimates upward

cards.subject: Analogous estimate
says: uses the actual result of a similar past project as the starting point
depends on how truly similar the earlier project was
cards.use: have delivered a near-identical site before and need a fast figure
not: sums task-level estimates

cards.subject: Parametric estimate
says: multiplies a measured unit rate by the quantity of work
relies on historical data for the cost per unit
cards.use: know the average cost per page or per integration from past work
not: relies on one similar past project

cards.subject: Three-point estimate
says: combines optimistic, most likely and pessimistic values
can weight the likely value more heavily than the extremes
cards.use: need to show uncertainty in a task rather than a single number
not: uses a single number agreed by the team

cards.subject: Contingency buffer
says: adds explicit time or cost to cover known uncertainty
is shown and managed rather than hidden
cards.use: expect some unknowns and want to cover them openly
not: adds hidden extra hours to each task

cards.subject: Hidden padding
says: adds secret margin inside each task estimate
makes it impossible to see or manage the real risk
cards.use: find each person adding a little extra to every task without telling anyone
not: is a visible buffer agreed with the client

cards.subject: Cone of uncertainty
says: shows that estimates are widest early and narrow as work progresses
argues for giving ranges at the start of a project
cards.use: asked for a single exact price on a vague first call
not: shows that estimates grow more accurate without any new information

cards.subject: Planning fallacy
says: is the habit of underestimating even when past projects ran long
is reduced by using real data from similar past work
cards.use: see the team keep promising dates that its own history shows are optimistic
not: is the habit of over-padding every estimate

cards.subject: Spike
says: is a short time-boxed investigation to reduce uncertainty
produces knowledge rather than a finished feature
cards.use: cannot estimate a task because of an unknown integration
not: is an urgent production fix

cards.subject: Fixed price
says: sets one agreed fee for a defined scope
puts the risk of overrun on the provider
cards.use: know the scope is stable and the client wants cost certainty
not: lets the client pay only for hours worked

cards.subject: Time and materials
says: bills for the hours worked and materials used
puts the risk of overrun on the client
cards.use: expect the scope to be unclear and to change as work proceeds
not: guarantees the client a fixed total

cards.subject: Capped time and materials
says: bills hours worked but never above an agreed ceiling
limits the client's exposure while keeping flexibility
cards.use: meet a client who wants flexibility but needs a maximum figure
not: bills a fixed fee whatever the hours

cards.subject: Retainer
says: reserves a block of time or availability for a regular fee
treats unused hours as lost or rolled over, depending on the terms
cards.use: meet a client who needs steady ongoing access to a team each month
not: charges only when a specific project is finished

cards.subject: Value-based pricing
says: sets the fee from the value the client gets rather than the cost of delivery
needs proof of the value the work will create
cards.use: expect the work to earn the client far more than the hours suggest
not: adds a fixed percentage to delivery cost

cards.subject: Subscription
says: charges a recurring fee for continued access to a packaged service
gives the provider predictable income
cards.use: sell a standard service that the client uses continuously
not: bills hours worked at the end of a project

cards.subject: Usage-based pricing
says: charges according to how much of the service is consumed
makes revenue vary with the client's activity
cards.use: see the cost to serve rise with the volume the client uses
not: charges the same monthly fee at any volume

cards.subject: Cost-plus pricing
says: adds a margin to the cost of delivery
ignores what the work is worth to the client
cards.use: want a simple price built from cost with an added margin
not: bases the fee on the client's expected benefit

cards.subject: Success fee
says: ties part of the fee to a result the client achieves
moves some outcome risk to the provider
cards.use: meet a client who will only pay if a measured result is reached
not: is paid whatever the result

cards.subject: Milestone billing
says: invoices when agreed milestones are reached
spreads payments across the project instead of one invoice at the end
cards.use: want to invoice in stages as work is accepted
not: bills the full amount before work starts

cards.subject: Price anchoring
says: sets a reference figure that shapes how later numbers are judged
is why showing the higher option first can change buyers' perception
cards.use: want a mid-priced package to look reasonable beside a premium one
not: lowers every price to the cheapest competitor

cards.subject: Gross margin
says: is revenue minus direct delivery cost, shown as a share of revenue
measures how much of each sale is left after delivering it
cards.use: want to know how much of a fee remains after the people who delivered it are paid
not: is the percentage added on top of cost

cards.subject: Markup
says: adds a percentage on top of cost to reach a price
gives a larger percentage figure than the margin for the same price
cards.use: need to turn a delivery cost into a price using a percentage on cost
not: is revenue minus cost divided by revenue

cards.subject: Utilisation rate
says: is billable hours as a share of available hours
drops when staff spend time on non-billable work
cards.use: need to know how much of the team's time earns revenue
not: is the share of billed work that gets paid

cards.subject: Realisation rate
says: compares what was billed with the value of time worked at standard rates
falls when work is discounted or written off
cards.use: find the team works full days but billings keep trailing hours worked
not: is billable hours divided by available hours

cards.subject: Blended rate
says: is the average hourly rate across a mixed team
moves when the mix of senior and junior time changes
cards.use: need one hourly figure for a team of different seniority
not: is the hourly rate of the most senior person

cards.subject: Effective hourly rate
says: divides the fee received by the hours actually spent
exposes unprofitable fixed-price projects
cards.use: want the real earning rate of a fixed-price project that overran
not: is the rate printed on the rate card

cards.subject: Cost to serve
says: is the total cost of supporting one client over a period
includes support, account management and overhead, not just build hours
cards.use: suspect a small client takes far more support than their fee covers
not: is the sale price of the package

cards.subject: Work in progress
says: is value of work done but not yet invoiced
grows when billing lags behind delivery and strains cash flow
cards.use: see delivered work pile up with no invoice issued
not: is money the client has already paid in advance

cards.subject: Capacity planning
says: compares the team's available hours with committed work
shows whether a new sale can be delivered on time
cards.use: are about to sign a project and need to know whether the team can absorb it
not: measures client satisfaction

cards.subject: Service level agreement
says: sets measurable service levels such as response times
defines remedies when levels are missed
cards.use: hear the client want response and availability promises in writing
not: lists the project deliverables and fees

cards.subject: Master services agreement
says: sets the general terms for all work between two parties
lets separate statements of work be added without renegotiating terms
cards.use: expect several engagements with the same client over time
not: fixes the price of one specific project

cards.subject: Non-disclosure agreement
says: obliges the parties to keep shared information confidential
is often signed before detailed discovery
cards.use: need to share sensitive information before agreeing a deal
not: transfers ownership of the work produced

cards.subject: IP ownership clause
says: states who owns the work product after delivery
is often tied to payment in full
cards.use: hear the client ask who owns the finished design and code
not: states how quickly defects will be fixed

cards.subject: Licence
says: grants permission to use something without transferring ownership
may be limited by time, purpose or territory
cards.use: let the client use a component while the provider keeps ownership
not: transfers full ownership to the client

cards.subject: Warranty
says: promises to fix defects found within a defined period after delivery
covers faults against the agreed specification, not new requests
cards.use: hear the client report a fault shortly after go-live
not: promises new features after launch

cards.subject: Termination clause
says: sets how and when either party may end the agreement
states notice periods and what happens to unpaid work
cards.use: need to know how a client can leave and what they owe when they do
not: describes how defects will be fixed

cards.subject: Acceptance criteria
says: are testable conditions a deliverable must meet to be accepted
prevent open-ended sign-off disputes
cards.use: want an objective test for when a deliverable counts as done
not: are the client's general wishes for the project

cards.subject: Limitation of liability
says: caps the damages one party can owe the other
protects the provider from losses far larger than the fee
cards.use: worry that a fault could create a claim much larger than the contract value
not: promises unlimited compensation for any loss

cards.subject: Indemnity
says: obliges one party to cover the other's losses from specified claims
is often used for third-party infringement claims
cards.use: are asked to cover the client against a claim that delivered work infringes someone's rights
not: caps the total damages payable

cards.subject: Data processing agreement
says: sets how a provider handles personal data on the client's behalf
is typically needed when the provider processes the client's personal data
cards.use: will host or process client customer data
not: describes the payment schedule

cards.subject: Proposal
says: presents the client's problem, the proposed solution, price and next steps
is shaped by what was learned in discovery
cards.use: need to put a full recommended solution in front of a client
not: is the signed contract

cards.subject: Quote
says: states a price for a clearly defined scope
may be only a few lines of scope and figures
cards.use: meet a client who only needs a price for a well-defined job
not: argues why the client should change strategy

cards.subject: Executive summary
says: gives the decision maker the problem, solution and price in a short page
is often the only part a senior reader fully reads
cards.use: expect the person who signs not to read the whole document
not: lists the detailed task plan

cards.subject: Validity period
says: states how long the quoted price and terms stay open
protects the provider from cost changes
cards.use: want the quoted price to expire if the client delays
not: states how long the project will take

cards.subject: Options page
says: offers two or three priced routes with different scope
moves the decision from yes-or-no to which-one
cards.use: want the client to choose between versions of the solution
not: presents a single price with no alternatives

cards.subject: Social proof
says: shows evidence from past clients such as case studies
reduces the buyer's perceived risk
cards.use: meet a prospect who is unsure whether you can deliver
not: lists the provider's internal costs

cards.subject: Concession trading
says: gives a discount or extra only in return for something from the buyer
keeps the price from being cut for free
cards.use: hear the buyer ask for a lower price at the negotiation stage
not: gives a discount to close quickly

cards.subject: Win-loss review
says: studies why proposals were won or lost
feeds findings back into pricing and positioning
cards.use: want to learn why recent bids keep losing to one competitor
not: measures client satisfaction after delivery

cards.subject: Lowball bid
says: wins work by pricing below real cost
risks a loss and pressure to cut quality or fight every change
cards.use: are tempted to underprice to win a competitive tender
not: sets a price that includes a healthy margin

cards.subject: Onboarding checklist
says: lists the access, contacts and information needed from the client at the start
reduces delay caused by missing inputs
cards.use: want to collect logins, brand assets and contacts at the outset
not: records faults found during testing

cards.subject: Kickoff meeting
says: aligns client and team on scope, roles, dates and communication
is held at the start of delivery
cards.use: are starting delivery and need everyone to agree the plan
not: is the final review before launch

cards.subject: Single point of contact
says: gives the client one named person for communication
prevents mixed messages from several team members
cards.use: find the client getting contradictory updates from different staff
not: gives every staff member direct client access

cards.subject: RACI matrix
says: assigns who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed
clarifies ownership of each task or decision
cards.use: find people unsure who makes the final call on an approval
not: lists the milestones and dates

cards.subject: Communication plan
says: sets who gets what updates, how often and through which channel
reduces surprises for the client
cards.use: hear the client complain that they never know progress
not: records the changes to scope

cards.subject: RAID log
says: records risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies
is reviewed regularly with the client
cards.use: want a single place to track what could go wrong and what is blocked
not: lists the agreed deliverables

cards.subject: Steering committee
says: brings senior client and provider leaders together to oversee a larger engagement
decides on escalated issues, scope and budget
cards.use: run a large engagement that needs senior-level oversight and decisions
not: is the daily team stand-up

cards.subject: User acceptance testing
says: lets the client test the deliverable against agreed criteria
ends with a sign-off or a list of defects to fix
cards.use: want the client to verify the work before it goes live
not: is testing done only by the provider's developers

cards.subject: QA checklist
says: lists the checks a deliverable must pass before it goes to the client
catches defects before the client sees them
cards.use: want a repeatable list to review the work before handing it over
not: is the client's wish list

cards.subject: Handover pack
says: gives the client the access, documentation and instructions to run what was delivered
includes training or a walk-through
cards.use: finish a project and see the client's team take over
not: is the signed proposal

cards.subject: Post-project review
says: looks back at what went well and badly after delivery
feeds lessons into estimates and process
cards.use: close a project and want the team to learn from it
not: is a review of the proposal before it is sent

cards.subject: Maintenance retainer
says: covers ongoing updates, fixes and monitoring for a regular fee
keeps delivered work healthy after launch
cards.use: want to keep a delivered site updated and supported each month
not: covers building brand-new projects

cards.subject: Support ticket
says: records one client request or fault with its status
gives a traceable history of the issue
cards.use: need every client request logged and followed
not: is a monthly invoice

cards.subject: Response time
says: is how fast the provider first replies to a request
starts the clock on the first acknowledgement, not the fix
cards.use: hear the client ask how fast someone will pick up their request
not: is how long the fix takes

cards.subject: Resolution time
says: is how long it takes to fix the problem
is usually longer than the first response target
cards.use: hear the client ask when the problem will be fully fixed
not: is how fast the first reply arrives

cards.subject: Severity level
says: ranks an issue by its impact on the client's business
sets the response target for that issue
cards.use: need to decide which of several faults to handle first
not: ranks clients by size

cards.subject: Service hours
says: state the days and times when support is staffed
are the window in which response targets count
cards.use: hear the client ask whether weekend problems will be handled
not: are the hours billed on a project

cards.subject: Uptime commitment
says: states the share of time a service should be available
usually excludes agreed maintenance windows
cards.use: hear the client need a measurable availability promise for hosting
not: is the target time to answer a ticket

cards.subject: Service credit
says: compensates the client with a credit when a service level is missed
is often the sole remedy for a missed uptime target
cards.use: see the service miss its stated availability
not: is a refund of the full contract

cards.subject: Escalation path
says: defines who an issue goes to when it is not resolved in time
names levels of seniority
cards.use: find a critical issue stuck with no one knowing who to call
not: is a list of the client's contacts

cards.subject: First-line support
says: handles routine requests and basic troubleshooting
passes complex issues to specialists
cards.use: need a first contact to resolve simple requests quickly
not: handles only the most complex engineering faults

cards.subject: Incident review
says: analyses a serious outage to find causes and actions
focuses on fixing the system, not blaming people
cards.use: come out of a major outage and want to prevent a repeat
not: assigns blame to the engineer on duty

cards.subject: Upsell
says: offers a higher tier or bigger version of what the client already buys
works best when tied to a need the client has shown
cards.use: meet a client who has outgrown their current package
not: offers a different service to a new buyer

cards.subject: Cross-sell
says: offers a different service to an existing client
builds on the trust already earned
cards.use: see that a hosting client could benefit from SEO
not: offers a bigger version of the same service

cards.subject: Renewal
says: extends a contract or subscription for another term
is easier when value has been shown during the term
cards.use: see a client's annual agreement close to ending
not: is a first sale to a new buyer

cards.subject: Churn
says: is clients leaving or cancelling over a period
reduces recurring revenue
cards.use: want to count how many clients stopped paying
not: is clients buying more

cards.subject: Client health score
says: combines signals such as usage, satisfaction and payment into one rating
flags at-risk accounts early
cards.use: want a quick way to see which accounts might leave
not: is the client's credit rating

cards.subject: Quarterly business review
says: is a regular meeting that shows the client the results delivered
creates a natural moment to plan upsell and renewal
cards.use: want to prove value to the client and plan the next period
not: is the first discovery call

cards.subject: Net revenue retention
says: measures revenue from existing clients including expansion and loss
can exceed 100 percent when upsell outweighs churn
cards.use: want to know whether existing clients are growing or shrinking in value
not: counts revenue from new clients

cards.subject: Early warning signal
says: is a behaviour such as slower replies or fewer logins that predicts churn
gives time to act before the client leaves
cards.use: notice a client stops joining calls and delays invoices
not: is the formal cancellation notice

cards.subject: Complaint acknowledgement
says: tells the client quickly that the complaint is heard
comes before any explanation or fix
cards.use: receive an angry email about a missed date
not: defends the team's decisions first

cards.subject: Root cause analysis
says: traces a failure back to the underlying cause
prevents the same complaint from recurring
cards.use: see the same type of complaint come up three times
not: fixes only the symptom the client noticed

cards.subject: Goodwill gesture
says: offers a small concession to repair trust after a failure
is given with a clear explanation and not as a habit
cards.use: want to repair the relationship after a service failure cost the client time
not: is a contractual entitlement

cards.subject: Service recovery paradox
says: describes clients who become more loyal after a well-handled failure than if none had occurred
does not justify causing failures on purpose
cards.use: hear someone argue that failing deliberately could build loyalty
not: says a failure always loses the client

cards.subject: Executive sponsor call
says: brings a senior leader into a troubled account to show commitment
is used when normal channels have not rebuilt trust
cards.use: see a key account threaten to leave after repeated problems
not: is the first routine status update

cards.subject: Subcontractor
says: is an outside provider who performs part of the delivery under the main supplier
remains the main supplier's responsibility to the client
cards.use: lack in-house skills for part of the project
not: is the client's own employee

cards.subject: White-label delivery
says: delivers work under the provider's own brand though another firm produces it
keeps the partner invisible to the client
cards.use: want to sell a service that a partner builds without showing their name
not: names the partner on every deliverable

cards.subject: Flow-down terms
says: pass the main contract's obligations, such as confidentiality and quality, to the subcontractor
stop gaps between what the provider promised and the subcontractor owes
cards.use: promised the client confidentiality that your subcontractor has not agreed to
not: remove liability from the main supplier

cards.subject: Subcontractor margin
says: is the difference between what the client pays and what the subcontractor charges
pays for coordination, risk and quality control
cards.use: are pricing work that a partner will build
not: is the subcontractor's profit alone

cards.subject: Partner due diligence
says: checks a partner's skills, references, security and finances before use
reduces the chance of poor quality reaching the client
cards.use: are about to rely on a new freelance team for client work
not: happens after the client complains

cards.subject: Partner quality gate
says: reviews partner output before it reaches the client
keeps one standard whoever produced the work
cards.use: receive white-label work with errors the client could have seen
not: is the partner's own internal review only

cards.subject: Key-person risk
says: arises when delivery depends on one individual
can cause delay or loss when that person is unavailable
cards.use: find that only one freelancer knows how a client's system works
not: comes from having too many specialists

cards.subject: Non-solicitation clause
says: stops a partner from approaching the provider's clients or staff
protects the client relationship in white-label arrangements
cards.use: worry a white-label partner might sell directly to your client
not: stops the client from changing provider

cards.subject: Single-supplier dependency
says: is reliance on one partner for a critical part of delivery
leaves the provider exposed if that partner fails or raises prices
cards.use: find that all your hosting depends on a single outside vendor
not: is using several suppliers for the same function

qa.q: What is the clearest difference between a service and a product?
qa.right: A service is delivered through work performed for the client, while a product is built once and sold repeatedly
wrong: A service always costs more than a product
A product is always digital and a service is always physical
A service has no price until the client approves it
qa.why: Services depend on delivery effort for each client; products scale as the same finished offer.

qa.q: What does a service catalogue do?
qa.right: Lists the services offered with descriptions and entry terms
wrong: Records every hour each person worked
Stores signed client contracts
Ranks clients by revenue
qa.why: A catalogue is the shared view of what can be bought.

qa.q: What is the main aim of a discovery call?
qa.right: To understand the client's goals, constraints and context before quoting
wrong: To close the sale on the first call
To present the full price list
To collect the first payment
qa.why: Discovery gathers facts so scope and price are based on the real need.

qa.q: In a fixed-price project, who carries the risk if the work takes longer than estimated?
qa.right: The provider
wrong: The client
Both sides equally, always
Nobody, because the price adjusts automatically
qa.why: A fixed fee means overrun cost falls on the provider unless a change is approved.

qa.q: In a time-and-materials project, who carries the main risk of overrun?
qa.right: The client, because they pay for the hours used
wrong: The provider, who must absorb extra hours
The subcontractor
Neither, because hours are capped by default
qa.why: Time and materials bills actual effort, so extra effort raises the client's bill.

qa.q: What is scope creep?
qa.right: Work growing beyond the agreed scope without matching changes to fee or time
wrong: A formal change to the agreed scope
A discount given to win a deal
A delay caused by the client paying late
qa.why: Uncontrolled growth is what makes it creep.

qa.q: Which action best fits a first reaction to an upset client's complaint?
qa.right: Acknowledge it quickly and tell them it is being looked at
wrong: Explain why the team was right
Wait until the cause is fully known before replying
Offer a refund straight away
qa.why: Prompt acknowledgement comes before explanation or remedy.

qa.q: What is the job of an exclusion in a statement of work?
qa.right: To state clearly what is not included
wrong: To state what the estimate assumes is true
To list the payment dates
To name who owns the work
qa.why: Exclusions remove doubt about out-of-scope work.

qa.q: What is an assumption in a scope document?
qa.right: A condition taken as true on which the estimate depends
wrong: A promise by the client to buy more
A feature added at no charge
A term that ends the contract
qa.why: If an assumption fails, the price or timeline may need to change.

qa.q: What does BANT check?
qa.right: Budget, authority, need and timeline
wrong: Brand, audience, niche and tone
Billing, accounts, notices and terms
Backlog, approvals, notes and tasks
qa.why: BANT is a quick qualification checklist.

qa.q: Which statement about response time and resolution time is correct?
qa.right: Response time is how fast the first reply comes, and resolution time is how long the fix takes
wrong: They mean the same thing
Response time is the time to fix, and resolution time is the time to reply
Both start only after the issue is fixed
qa.why: They measure different points in handling an issue.

qa.q: What does a change order do?
qa.right: Records signed approval of a priced scope change
wrong: Reports a bug found in testing
Replaces the whole statement of work
Cancels the project
qa.why: It makes the extra cost and time agreed in writing.

qa.q: A retainer is best described as:
qa.right: A recurring fee that reserves time or availability
wrong: A single payment on completion
A fee that depends on the result achieved
A deposit that is refunded at the end
qa.why: A retainer buys ongoing access, not a one-off outcome.

qa.q: What is utilisation rate?
qa.right: Billable hours as a share of available hours
wrong: Billed amount as a share of the value of time worked
Profit as a share of revenue
Hours worked divided by the project budget
qa.why: Utilisation shows how much available time earns revenue.

qa.q: Why do acceptance criteria matter in a contract?
qa.right: They give an objective test for when a deliverable is accepted
wrong: They set the price of each deliverable
They limit the provider's liability
They state how long the contract lasts
qa.why: Without them sign-off can become a matter of opinion.

qa.q: Which is true of gross margin versus markup on the same price?
qa.right: Margin is calculated on revenue and markup on cost, so the markup percentage is the larger figure
wrong: Markup is calculated on revenue and margin on cost
They always give the same percentage
Markup is always smaller than margin
qa.why: For a cost of 80 and a price of 100, margin is 20 percent and markup is 25 percent.

qa.q: When is a bottom-up estimate more appropriate than an analogous one?
qa.right: When the tasks are known and can be listed individually
wrong: When the project is very unlike anything done before and has no detail
When the client wants an answer in five minutes
When the budget is already fixed
qa.why: Bottom-up adds task-level estimates and is more accurate when tasks are known.

qa.q: What does a three-point estimate give that a single number does not?
qa.right: A view of uncertainty through optimistic, likely and pessimistic values
wrong: A guarantee of the delivery date
A fixed price
A way to avoid contingency
qa.why: Three values show the spread of the estimate.

qa.q: What makes a contingency buffer different from hidden padding?
qa.right: A buffer is visible and managed, while padding is concealed inside task estimates
wrong: A buffer is always larger
Padding is approved by the client while a buffer is not
There is no difference
qa.why: Visible buffers allow the real risk to be discussed and controlled.

qa.q: For which situation is value-based pricing most suitable?
qa.right: A small piece of work that could earn the client many times its cost
wrong: A commodity service compared on price by every buyer
A job that is paid for at cost with a markup
A support ticket with a fixed response time
qa.why: Value-based pricing depends on a large benefit to the client.

qa.q: What risk does cost-plus pricing carry?
qa.right: It ignores the value to the client and can leave money on the table or price out the sale
wrong: It always loses money
It makes the client carry all delivery risk
It cannot be used with a fixed fee
qa.why: Cost-plus looks inward at cost rather than outward at value.

qa.q: What does capped time and materials protect?
qa.right: The client from paying more than an agreed ceiling
wrong: The provider from any overrun
The client from paying for any hours
The provider from scope changes
qa.why: The cap limits exposure while keeping the flexibility of hourly billing.

qa.q: What does a master services agreement allow?
qa.right: Separate statements of work to be added under standing general terms
wrong: A single project to be priced without scope
The client to skip acceptance testing
Fixed fees to change automatically
qa.why: It saves renegotiating terms for each engagement.

qa.q: What is the purpose of a RACI matrix?
qa.right: To show who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed for each task or decision
wrong: To track hours worked per person
To record defects found
To rank clients
qa.why: RACI removes confusion about ownership.

qa.q: What is the value of a client health score?
qa.right: It combines signals into a rating that flags at-risk accounts early
wrong: It sets the price for renewal
It records payments received
It replaces client meetings
qa.why: Early flags give time to act before the client leaves.

qa.q: Why add a flow-down clause to a subcontract?
qa.right: So the subcontractor is bound by the obligations the provider made to the client
wrong: So the client can contact the subcontractor directly
So the subcontractor can set its own terms
So the provider is released from responsibility
qa.why: Without it the provider can owe duties that nobody downstream is bound to meet.

qa.q: What is the main difference between a defect and a change?
qa.right: A defect fails the agreed specification and is fixed under warranty, while a change adds to the agreed scope
wrong: A defect is always minor and a change is always major
A change is free and a defect is paid
They are treated the same way
qa.why: The agreed specification decides which it is.

qa.q: What does realisation rate reveal that utilisation does not?
qa.right: How much of the time worked was billed at full value
wrong: How many hours were available
How many clients are active
How many tickets were closed
qa.why: Discounts and write-offs lower realisation even when utilisation is high.

qa.q: What does net revenue retention above 100 percent mean?
qa.right: Expansion from existing clients outweighs the revenue lost to churn and downgrades
wrong: No client left
New clients exceeded the target
Prices rose for everybody
qa.why: It measures the existing client base, not new sales.

qa.q: Why do many providers sell a paid discovery before a large project?
qa.right: To scope and estimate an unclear project safely and give the client a usable output
wrong: To collect a deposit without committing to build
To avoid signing a contract
To skip the proposal
qa.why: It reduces the risk of guessing a price for an unclear scope.

qa.q: What is the main danger of a lowball bid?
qa.right: It wins work that loses money or leads to cut quality and fights over every change
wrong: It always loses the tender
It gives the client too much power
It breaks confidentiality
qa.why: Underpricing pushes pain into delivery.

qa.q: What is the point of concession trading in negotiation?
qa.right: A discount or extra is given only in return for something such as longer term or faster payment
wrong: Concessions are offered quickly to close
Price is never discussed
The client makes all concessions
qa.why: Trading keeps a concession from being a free reduction.

qa.q: What does an indemnity clause do?
qa.right: Obliges one party to cover the other's losses from specified claims
wrong: Caps the total fees payable
Sets the support response time
States when the contract ends
qa.why: It allocates risk for named third-party claims.

qa.q: A lead on a first call refuses to share any goals and asks only for the cheapest price. What should you do first?
qa.right: Ask what outcome they want and what budget range they have, and treat it as a possible red flag
wrong: Send your lowest price
Send a full proposal immediately
Offer a free month to win them
qa.why: Without goals or budget you cannot scope; refusing to share is a warning sign.

qa.q: A client emails asking for an extra feature that is not in the signed scope, and the team lead says 'it's quick, just do it'. What should happen?
qa.right: Assess the impact and raise a change request before starting
wrong: Do it silently to keep the client happy
Refuse and ignore the email
Start now and invoice at the end of the project
qa.why: Change control protects both sides and avoids silent absorption.

qa.q: A fixed-price project is two weeks late because the client has not supplied content. What is your strongest position?
qa.right: Point to the client dependency and assumption in the statement of work and agree a revised date or change
wrong: Absorb the cost to avoid conflict
Stop work without telling the client
Switch to time and materials without discussion
qa.why: A written dependency is the basis for adjusting time or price.

qa.q: A client says the new contact form 'is broken' because it does not send a copy to a second address nobody asked for. How should you classify this?
qa.right: As a change, because it adds to the agreed specification
wrong: As a warranty defect to fix free
As scope creep by the provider
As gold plating
qa.why: The agreed specification determines whether it is a defect.

qa.q: A prospect with a small budget wants a bespoke platform. What is the best response?
qa.right: Offer a smaller productised option or a phased scope that fits the budget
wrong: Quote the bespoke price anyway
Accept the budget and deliver the full platform
Decline without explanation
qa.why: Fitting scope to budget keeps the deal and the margin.

qa.q: A client wants an exact price after a ten-minute call on a vague idea. What is the best response?
qa.right: Give a range with stated assumptions, or propose a paid discovery to define scope
wrong: Give one exact fixed price now
Refuse to give any figure
Double the price to be safe
qa.why: Early estimates need ranges because of the cone of uncertainty.

qa.q: Two of your developers each add a few extra hours to every task 'just in case'. What is the problem?
qa.right: The padding is hidden, so the real risk cannot be seen or managed
wrong: The estimates are now exact
The client will be undercharged
It saves the project manager time
qa.why: Use a visible contingency instead.

qa.q: A client has been quietly receiving small favours from the team for months and now expects them as standard. What should you do?
qa.right: Record the extras, show their value and agree whether to charge or include them in a retainer
wrong: Stop all favours immediately without telling them
Continue forever
Bill the client for all past favours at once
qa.why: Silent absorption sets precedent; make it visible and decide.

qa.q: A client's site went down and the retainer promises a one-hour response. You reply in forty minutes but the fix takes six hours. Was the response level met?
qa.right: Yes, the response target was met, though resolution was separate
wrong: No, because the fix took six hours
No, because the reply was not a fix
Only if the client agrees
qa.why: Response time measures the first reply, not the fix.

qa.q: A white-label partner delivers work with visible errors the day before the deadline. What control would have prevented this?
qa.right: A quality gate that reviews partner output before it reaches the client
wrong: A larger contingency in the price
A longer proposal
A lower subcontractor margin
qa.why: A gate catches partner errors before the client sees them.

qa.q: A fixed-price web project overran and its effective hourly rate is far below the rate card. What should you check first?
qa.right: Whether scope grew without change orders and whether the estimate omitted tasks
wrong: Whether the team worked too few hours
Whether the client paid late
Whether the rate card is too high
qa.why: Overrun on fixed price usually traces to unmanaged scope or missing tasks.

qa.q: A client is paying on time but has stopped joining calls and logging in. What is the best next step?
qa.right: Treat it as an early warning signal and contact them to check value and needs
wrong: Wait until they cancel
Raise their price
Send the renewal invoice early
qa.why: Behaviour change often precedes churn.

qa.q: A key account complains for the third time about missed dates. Normal updates have not helped. What is the strongest response?
qa.right: Run a root cause analysis and bring a senior sponsor into a recovery call with a plan
wrong: Send another apology email
Offer a discount and say nothing more
Reassign the account without telling them
qa.why: Repeated failure needs cause analysis and visible senior commitment.

qa.q: A large buyer insists on its own contract and a security questionnaire for a small web project. Which tier approach fits?
qa.right: Treat it as enterprise: involve procurement and review whether the margin covers the extra overhead
wrong: Refuse, because it is not in the catalogue
Skip the questionnaire to save time
Accept all terms without review
qa.why: Enterprise buyers bring extra process cost that must be priced.

qa.q: A sales colleague offers a client a 20 percent discount unprompted to close a deal. What should you say?
qa.right: Trade it for something, such as a longer term or faster payment
wrong: Approve it, since closing matters most
Reject any discount ever
Offer 40 percent so the client feels special
qa.why: Free discounts teach clients to ask for more.

qa.q: Your only freelancer who understands a client's automation workflow becomes unavailable. Which risk is this?
qa.right: Key-person risk
wrong: Scope creep
Gold plating
Churn
qa.why: Delivery depended on a single individual.

qa.q: A client asks you to guarantee that their new site will double their leads. What is the best response?
qa.right: Agree measurable success metrics and what you control, and avoid guaranteeing outcomes outside your control
wrong: Guarantee it to win the work
Refuse to discuss results
Say results cannot be measured
qa.why: Outcomes depend on factors beyond the provider; metrics should be agreed.

qa.q: A client wants to cancel their monthly retainer two weeks before the term ends. What should you check first?
qa.right: The termination and notice terms in the agreement
wrong: Whether the client is allowed to pay less
The support ticket history only
The competitor's price list
qa.why: The contract decides notice and what is owed.

qa.q: Your team's utilisation is high but profit is falling. Which metric should you look at?
qa.right: Realisation rate, to see if work is being discounted or written off
wrong: Churn only
Number of leads
Number of tickets
qa.why: High hours with low billing points to realisation problems.

qa.q: A client demands a fixed price for an AI-automation project whose data sources are not yet known. What is the safest approach?
qa.right: Sell a paid discovery or a capped time-and-materials phase, then fix the price for the remainder
wrong: Quote a fixed price for everything
Refuse the project
Quote time and materials with no cap and no review
qa.why: Unknowns should be reduced before fixing a price.

qa.q: A subcontractor wants a clause letting them contact your clients directly. What should you do?
qa.right: Reject it and include a non-solicitation clause
wrong: Accept, since they are a partner
Allow it only for small clients
Ask the client to approve it
qa.why: Direct contact would put your client relationship at risk.

qa.q: A client threatens legal action over an outage and claims losses far above the contract fee. Which contract term do you rely on first?
qa.right: The limitation of liability
wrong: The payment terms
The kickoff plan
The service catalogue
qa.why: The cap defines the maximum damages that can be claimed.

qa.q: A client's contract is up for renewal. Net revenue retention is above 100 percent but several small accounts left. What does this suggest?
qa.right: Larger accounts expanded enough to offset the loss, so check why small accounts leave
wrong: Churn is no longer a concern
Prices are too high everywhere
Support is performing perfectly
qa.why: A healthy aggregate can hide a segment problem.

qa.q: A client says their SLA was breached after a planned weekend maintenance window took the site offline for two hours. What do you check?
qa.right: Whether the agreed maintenance window is excluded from the uptime commitment
wrong: Whether the client was happy
Whether the site is fast
Whether the invoice was paid
qa.why: Agreed maintenance windows are normally excluded from availability.

qa.q: A client asks which package fits a start-up that wants to test its idea cheaply. Which catalogue concept helps?
qa.right: A free or semi-free tier to build trust before a paid package
wrong: An enterprise tier
A custom tier with negotiated terms
A lowball bid
qa.why: A free entry offer lets the client try before committing.
